issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life not worth living anymore' suggests a marked hopeless/depressive or self-destructive appraisal. The rest of the selected items center on fragmented trauma memory and avoidance/social distraction, without other items indicating pervasive defeat, guilt, permanent damage, or a threat-related meaning that would make this severe appraisal cohere strongly.

vignette: Daniel, a 35-year-old Latin American musician, came to therapy after months of trying to keep his life looking normal since a road accident that had nearly killed him. He had been on his way home from a late-night gig when a truck ran a red light and slammed into his car, leaving him trapped, pinned, and waiting for help while sirens echoed somewhere beyond the twisted metal. He remembered the crush of the seatbelt, the smell of gasoline, and then only disconnected flashes: a shard of broken windshield glittering in the dark, a paramedic’s glove, his own voice shouting once and then fading. When he tried to remember the full sequence on purpose, it would not come; he was left with pieces that would not join up, and the missing parts felt more alarming than the fragments themselves. Daniel spoke of the crash as something deeply unfair, something that should have been prevented and for which nothing had ever truly been done. Because he kept telling himself the accident had been unjust and that he should never have been put in that situation, his mind seemed to snag on the worst pieces of it; when he tried to remember, the scene came back in broken flashes rather than a clean sequence, as if the belief itself made the memory harder to hold together. He had come to believe that the accident had destroyed the life he had built, and that anger sat close to the surface in him; he feared that if he let himself fully think about what happened, he would lose control of that rage and do something terrible. In the weeks after the collision, Daniel began arranging his days around other people. He made sure there were always bandmates, friends, cousins, or neighbors around him, filling the apartment with noise and company so he would not be left alone with his thoughts. He accepted every invitation, lingered after rehearsals, stayed in diners long after meals were finished, and kept his phone busy with calls and messages. He did not want to talk about the accident or what came after it, and when anyone asked, he changed the subject, joked, or left the room. He told himself that conversation would only open the door to the anger he was trying to contain. The more he sensed the anger under the surface, the more insistently he stayed surrounded by people, as if constant socialising could keep him from the parts of himself he no longer trusted. At the same time, the way the memory came to him made it harder to live with. Because he could not deliberately pull the crash into a clear sequence, Daniel filled in the gaps with his own fear, and what remained incomplete took on a punishing meaning. The unfinished fragments made him more certain that the event had ruined everything: if even his mind could not hold the whole story together, then the accident must have been as catastrophic as he felt. The missing pieces also fed his suspicion that something inside him had gone permanently wrong. He began to watch himself for signs of anger, convinced that he might suddenly lose control, and that belief made him even more determined not to sit still with the memory. He avoided thinking about the night of the crash, but that effort had its own cost. The more he tried not to go there, the less coherent the memory became, and the more it seemed to confirm that the event was beyond repair and beyond justice. Daniel’s musical work and home life became the settings for this pattern. In rehearsal spaces, backstage rooms, and at home after his wife had gone to bed, he worked hard to keep moving, keep talking, keep the room occupied. If the conversation slowed, he reached for another story, another drink, another reason to stay with someone. Yet each burst of company left him less able to settle the fragments of the accident into words or sequence, and the memory stayed just out of reach. That, in turn, made the injustice and the sense of ruin feel even larger. He said he could not understand how his life, once built around music, family, and late-night energy, could have been broken so violently, and he was frightened by how readily his mind returned to the thought that everything had been taken from him. By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the cycle. He no longer trusted quiet moments, and he was afraid that if he kept avoiding the memory he would remain trapped in the same incomplete, angry state, but if he opened it up he might be overwhelmed by rage he could not control. Keeping the crash unspoken in that way had its own cost: because he never sat with it long enough to tell it through from beginning to end, the memory stayed jagged and incomplete, surfacing later only in disconnected pieces. What brought him in was the realization that his constant company-seeking, his refusal to speak about the crash, and his efforts to avoid thinking about it were no longer just helping him get through the day; they were keeping the accident alive in pieces that felt more threatening than the truth. He hoped therapy might help him make sense of what happened, and he was most afraid that the life he believed had been destroyed would stay that way forever.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs about the accident, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals drive the fragmented/incomplete memory.
The vignette describes fragmented memory leading to worse beliefs about the crash, but it does not clearly show the memory causing the negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows avoidance and constant company-seeking, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies cause the memory to become less coherent or more fragmented.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette shows negative beliefs about the accident, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals drive the fragmented/incomplete memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette describes fragmented memory leading to worse beliefs about the crash, but it does not clearly show the memory causing the negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette shows avoidance and constant company-seeking, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies cause the memory to become less coherent or more fragmented.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
